A concept with no attempt is unmeasured; it is not scored zero and is not averaged in. Evidence halves in weight every 30 days, and self-graded evidence counts at 0.5 of a server-graded answer.

concept.explanation: A variable in Python is a name attached to an object, not a box that holds a value. `a = [1, 2]` binds the name `a` to a list object. `b = a` binds a second name to the same object, so a change made through `b` is visible through `a`. Rebinding — `a = [3]` — attaches `a` to a different object and leaves `b` alone. Most confusion about Python 'pass by reference' comes from mixing up rebinding and mutation.
concept.subject: Python
concept.summary: A name bound to a value, and why rebinding is not the same as mutating.
concept.title: Variables and names

lesson.application: When a function seems to change a caller's variable 'for no reason', check whether both names point at the same mutable object.
lesson.example:
a = [1]
b = a
b.append(2)
print(a)  # [1, 2] — same object
a = [9]
print(b)  # [1, 2] — rebinding a did not touch b
lesson.explanation: Binding attaches a name to an object. Rebinding moves the name; mutation changes the object both names still refer to.
lesson.hook: Two names, one list, and a bug that looks impossible.
lesson.recap: Rebinding ≠ mutation. `is` compares identity; `==` compares value.
lesson.title: Names, not boxes

openings.idea: A flank first move that fights for d5 without occupying the centre. Often transposes into Queen's Gambit or Indian structures - so naming it early is a choice, not a distinction.
openings.name: English Opening

openings.idea: Black controls e4 from a distance and delays committing pawns to the centre. Flexible, and the gateway to the King's Indian and Nimzo-Indian structures.
openings.name: Indian Game

openings.idea: Black answers the centre with a flank pawn, unbalancing the position from move one. The trade is space for counterplay on the queenside.
openings.name: Sicilian Defence

openings.idea: White opens the centre and gets a knight to d4; Black accepts a slightly cramped but solid position with play against the d4 knight.
openings.moves_san: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4
openings.moves_uci: e2e4 c7c5 g1f3 d7d6 d2d4 c5d4 f3d4
openings.name: Sicilian, Classical

openings.idea: The most heavily analysed line in chess. a7-a6 controls b5 and prepares ...e5 or ...b5, keeping maximum flexibility.
openings.moves_san: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6
openings.moves_uci: e2e4 c7c5 g1f3 d7d6 d2d4 c5d4 f3d4 g8f6 b1c3 a7a6
openings.name: Sicilian, Najdorf

openings.idea: The bishop takes the a2-g8 diagonal before the position closes. Direct, principled and the best place for a beginner to learn development.
openings.name: Italian Game

openings.idea: Black develops and hits e4 rather than defending passively. White must decide between quiet development and the sharp Ng5 lines.
openings.moves_san: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6
openings.moves_uci: e2e4 e7e5 g1f3 b8c6 f1c4 g8f6
openings.name: Italian, Two Knights Defence

openings.idea: The pin on c6 is tested immediately. The resulting endgames are famously hard to win against a prepared opponent - a good practical choice.
openings.moves_san: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 Nf6
openings.moves_uci: e2e4 e7e5 g1f3 b8c6 f1b5 g8f6
openings.name: Ruy Lopez, Berlin Defence

openings.idea: A pawn offer on c4. Accepting does not win a pawn cleanly, because White regains it with e2-e3 and a bishop on the long diagonal.
openings.name: Queen's Gambit

openings.idea: Black holds the centre rather than grabbing material. The cost is a passive light-squared bishop, which shapes the whole middlegame.
openings.name: Queen's Gambit Declined

lessons.title: Starting, and keeping a routine alive

topics.title: Sustainable time management and scheduling
Reducing procrastination with task shaping, prompts and implementation intentions
Maintaining a minimum viable learning routine during busy periods

lessons.model: Procrastination is usually a property of the task as shaped, not of the person: the next action is too big, or too vague, to begin. Shaping it into a first step you could do in two minutes, attached to a cue that already exists, removes the decision — and decisions are the expensive part.
lessons.when_to_use: Starting anything you have postponed twice, and rebuilding after a disrupted week.
lessons.when_not_to_use: When the task is genuinely the wrong task. A better cue for work you should not be doing is an efficient way to waste a month.
lessons.worked_example: "Revise statistics" becomes "open the chapter 4 problem set and copy the first question onto paper, at 19:00, at the kitchen table, after the plates are cleared". The cue is the cleared table; the first step needs no judgement.
lessons.exercise: Take one postponed task. Write the two-minute first step, the cue that triggers it, and the smallest version of the session you would still count as having happened on a bad day.
lessons.judging_results: Count starts per week and the minutes from cue to first action. A routine that survives your worst week is working; one that only survives good weeks is a fair-weather schedule.
lessons.traps: Building the minimum viable routine out of optimism; treating a missed day as evidence that the routine failed rather than that it was too large.

retrieval_check.question: Why does a two-minute first step work when a 90-minute session does not?
criteria: Names that the barrier is starting (decision and task size), not capacity
Connects it to a cue or implementation intention
Mentions that the session still needs an objective and a stopping condition

lessons.title: The growth zone, and what makes a session a session

topics.title: Entering an appropriately challenging growth zone
Designing a productive session with a clear objective and stopping condition

lessons.model: Difficulty has a productive band: hard enough that retrieval is effortful, easy enough that success is frequent. A session earns the name by declaring an objective and a stopping condition before it starts, so it ends because it is finished rather than because attention ran out.
lessons.when_to_use: Every deliberate session; especially when choosing what to work on next.
lessons.when_not_to_use: For first exposure to a procedure where errors are unsafe. Blocked practice at low difficulty is correct there, and the growth zone waits.
lessons.worked_example: Objective: "explain the mechanism of demand paging without notes". Stopping condition: "twenty minutes, or one uninterrupted explanation, whichever comes first". Difficulty chosen so the first attempt likely fails partway — which is the useful outcome, not a setback.
lessons.exercise: Write tomorrow's session as an objective, a stopping condition and a difficulty estimate. Afterwards, record whether the difficulty was right.
lessons.judging_results: If you succeeded without effort, the difficulty was below the band. If you could not start producing anything, it was above it. Adjust one notch.
lessons.traps: Objectives that describe activity ("revise chapter 3") rather than production; stopping conditions that are clock-only when the work is not time-shaped.

retrieval_check.question: What are the two things a session must declare before it starts, and why?
criteria: Objective stated as something produced, not an activity
Stopping condition stated in advance
Gives a reason: the session ends on completion, not on exhaustion

lessons.title: Spacing, and choosing when to review

topics.title: The spacing effect and spacing schedules
Retrieval scheduling from performance, importance, deadline and elapsed time

lessons.model: Memory strengthens more when retrieval happens after forgetting has begun than while the material is still fresh. Spacing is therefore not a convenience — the gap is the mechanism. But the right gap depends on why you are reviewing: a deadline, an exam date, or a decay risk.
lessons.when_to_use: Any material you intend to keep beyond the week you learned it.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Immediately before first understanding. Spacing something you never encoded just schedules confusion at intervals.
lessons.worked_example: A procedure learned Monday with an assessment in six weeks: first retrieval Wednesday, second in eight days, then stretched while each success holds. A high-importance concept due in three weeks gets shorter gaps than a low-importance one with no deadline.
lessons.exercise: Take three things you learned this week. Give each a next retrieval date and one sentence saying which of performance, importance, deadline or elapsed time set it.
lessons.judging_results: Track recall at each interval. Success at a stretched interval is evidence the gap was right; failure twice at the same interval says the gap was too long.
lessons.traps: Reviewing on a fixed weekly grid regardless of the material; letting the app or the calendar own a decision you should be able to explain.

retrieval_check.question: Name the four things that should change how soon you review something.
criteria: Performance on the last retrieval
Importance of the material
Deadline or assessment date
Time elapsed since the last successful retrieval

lessons.title: Interleaving, recognition, and practice under the clock

topics.title: Declarative versus procedural interleaving
Recognition versus recall, and when each is appropriate
Retrieval under time constraints

lessons.model: Interleaving mixes two similar things so that telling them apart becomes the work. It helps declarative material where discrimination is the difficulty, and helps procedural material when the choice of procedure is the skill. Recognition is a weaker test than recall and is only appropriate when the real task is recognising.
lessons.when_to_use: Once each item is understood separately and the confusion between them is the problem.
lessons.when_not_to_use: During first instruction, or when a procedure must be executed safely and consistently. Blocked practice builds the unit; interleaving tests it.
lessons.worked_example: Two statistical tests with similar assumptions: blocking teaches each one, then interleaving presents unlabelled problems so choosing becomes the skill. A timed set follows only once choice is reliable, because speed is tested last.
lessons.exercise: Build a ten-item mix from two topics you keep confusing. Do it once untimed and once timed; note whether errors are of choice or of execution.
lessons.judging_results: Errors of choice mean the discrimination is not built; errors of execution mean it is built but not automatic. Those need different practice.
lessons.traps: Confusing the discomfort of interleaving with evidence that it is working; adding a timer before the choice is reliable and recording the resulting panic as a comprehension problem.

retrieval_check.question: When is recognition the right test, and when is it a way of avoiding the test?
criteria: Recognition is right when the real task is recognising
It is a way of avoiding the test when the real task is producing
Says recall should be the default once the material is known at all

lessons.title: Prompts, cards, and one change at a time

topics.title: Prompt design, error correction and delayed retesting
Marginal gains: one high-value improvement at a time
Flashcard triage to remove redundant or low-value cards

lessons.model: A prompt should demand production, not recognition, unless recognition is the target. Every error found by retrieval gets corrected and then retested later, or it is being rehearsed. Cards that have become trivial or that duplicate another are removed, because cheap cards are how a deck becomes unmaintainable.
lessons.when_to_use: Reviewing a deck, designing prompts, and choosing what to improve next.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Changing several parts of your method at once. Then no result tells you which change did anything.
lessons.worked_example: A card reading "Define osmosis" is rewritten as "A cell is placed in distilled water — explain what happens to it, and why". Six duplicated cards are deleted. One change this fortnight: prompt quality, not card count.
lessons.exercise: Audit twenty cards: mark each as recall, recognition or unclear; rewrite the unclear ones; delete the duplicates. Pick exactly one further change to test.
lessons.judging_results: Compare delayed performance on the rewritten cards against the untouched ones two weeks later. Improvement on prompts that were not changed is not attributable to the change.
lessons.traps: Improving everything simultaneously and crediting the improvement; keeping a card because it took effort to make, which is sunk cost with a nicer name.

retrieval_check.question: Why does an error found by retrieval have to be retested later?
criteria: Correction alone does not replace the original trace
It only becomes evidence once it survives a later, unsupported retrieval

lessons.title: Priming with a time box, and scheduling the two halves

topics.title: Prestudy and priming
Scheduling encoding and retrieval sessions

lessons.model: Priming works when it ends: a few minutes to activate prior knowledge, name a question and check prerequisites. Encoding and retrieval are separate sessions in a well-run week, because doing them together hides which one is producing the result.
lessons.when_to_use: Before new material, and when a week's plan is being laid out.
lessons.when_not_to_use: As a substitute for starting. If priming has run past its budget twice, it is the work you are avoiding.
lessons.worked_example: Six minutes with a visible timer: three things I already know about inflation, one question this reading should answer, one thing I need first. Then the reading. The retrieval session is on Thursday, not at the end of the reading.
lessons.exercise: Prime for six minutes before your next study block and write the question. Book the retrieval session for a different day before you begin.
lessons.judging_results: The test of priming is whether the subsequent session started faster and produced better questions — not whether the priming felt productive.
lessons.traps: Priming without a timer; scheduling encoding and retrieval in the same sitting and then wondering why nothing survives a week.

retrieval_check.question: What are the three outputs of a priming session, and what bounds it?
criteria: Prior knowledge activated, a question to answer, prerequisites checked
A time box, so it cannot become preparation

lessons.title: Live explanations, and notes worth keeping

topics.title: Learning during lectures, seminars, classes and live explanations
Effective note-taking and reference capture

lessons.model: In a live explanation you cannot pause the speaker, so the useful activity is capturing questions and structure, not transcription. A reference note earns its place by answering a question someone will ask later; if it cannot answer one, it is a souvenir.
lessons.when_to_use: Lectures, seminars, tutorials and any explanation delivered at someone else's pace.
lessons.when_not_to_use: When the material is recorded and you will rewatch it. Then the live note is duplicated, and the rewatch is better spent doing retrieval.
lessons.worked_example: One page split in two: structure on the left (what the argument's parts are), questions on the right (where I lost the thread). Afterwards, two minutes to convert the questions into a retrieval prompt. The note is filed with the question it answers.
lessons.exercise: Take one note you already have. Write at its top the question it answers. If no question fits, retire it.
lessons.judging_results: A note is working if you can answer its question from it cold. Notes that are never reopened are not evidence of note-taking skill.
lessons.traps: Transcribing instead of listening; filing by date rather than by question; judging a note by its length.

retrieval_check.question: What makes a reference note worth keeping?
criteria: It answers a specific future question
It carries enough context (source, definition, mechanism) to be usable alone
Volume is explicitly rejected as the measure

lessons.title: High-yield memorisation, mechanisms, and examinations

topics.title: High-yield memorisation
Explaining mechanisms and resolving misconceptions
Preparation for written and oral examinations

lessons.model: Memorise what must be produced exactly and cannot be derived; build a mechanism for everything else so the detail has somewhere to attach. Misconceptions do not fade when the correct statement is repeated — they fade when the model that produced them is contradicted explicitly.
lessons.when_to_use: Preparing for written or oral assessment, and whenever an error keeps returning.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Memorising a derivation you do not understand. It survives exactly until the question is phrased differently.
lessons.worked_example: For an oral exam on aetiology: the mechanism explained aloud in ninety seconds, then the four facts that must be exact, then one question answered under time. The misconception you held is written down beside the correction so it can be tested again.
lessons.exercise: Write your three most persistent misconceptions and, for each, the model that produced them. Then write the correction as a change to that model.
lessons.judging_results: A misconception is resolved when a question designed to trigger it produces the corrected model unprompted. Feeling corrected is not the test.
lessons.traps: Rereading the correct version and assuming the wrong one left; preparing for the exam you would set rather than the one that will be given.

retrieval_check.question: How do you resolve a misconception, as distinct from learning the right answer?
criteria: Identify the model that produced the error
Contradict that model explicitly
Retest with a question designed to trigger the old error

lessons.title: Cues, routines, and the environment that decides for you

topics.title: Habit formation: cues, routines and reliable triggers
Implementation intentions and environment design

lessons.model: A habit is a cue, a routine and a consequence, and the cue is the part worth designing. Environment design beats willpower because it removes choices: the book on the desk, the phone in another room.
lessons.when_to_use: Building any behaviour you want to happen without deciding each time.
lessons.when_not_to_use: For behaviour you do not actually want repeated. An effective cue for the wrong routine is a problem, not progress.
lessons.worked_example: Implementation intention: "After I clear the plates, I open the problem set at the kitchen table." Environment: the folder is on the table, the phone charges in the hall. Two changes, both to the setting rather than to resolve.
lessons.exercise: Write one implementation intention in the after-I-X-I-will-Y form, and change one thing in the room to match it.
lessons.judging_results: Count how often the routine happened without a decision being made. If every instance required resolve, the cue is not working yet.
lessons.traps: Designing cues that depend on a tidy house, an empty calendar or a good mood; adding habits until the cue chain collides with itself.

retrieval_check.question: Why is the cue the part of a habit worth designing?
criteria: It is what starts the routine without a decision
Environment design removes the choice, which is what willpower was compensating for

lessons.title: Unlearning, slips, and the all-or-nothing trap

topics.title: Unlearning habits that make learning less effective
Handling slips without abandoning the system
Perfectionism and the all-or-nothing trap
Measuring whether a habit improves outcomes, not only streak length

lessons.model: An unhelpful habit is replaced, not deleted: the cue stays and a competing response takes the routine's place. A slip is data about the design, not a verdict, and a system that cannot survive a slip is designed for someone who does not exist.
lessons.when_to_use: After the second slip, and any time a habit's value is being inferred from its streak.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Turning every interruption into a redesign. One broken day is noise; three in a fortnight is a pattern.
lessons.worked_example: The cue "opening the laptop in the evening" led to scrolling. Competing response: the laptop stays closed and the paper notebook comes out. Two slips in ten days were followed by one question — what preceded them — not by abandoning the routine.
lessons.exercise: Name one habit you want to unlearn, its cue, and a competing response that fits the same cue. Then write what you will do after the next slip.
lessons.judging_results: Measure outcomes, not streaks: did the reading happen more often, was the work better, did the sessions get easier to start? A 40-day streak of a habit that changes nothing is 40 days spent.
lessons.traps: All-or-nothing restart ("I'll begin again on Monday"); measuring the streak because it is easy to measure and then optimising for it.

retrieval_check.question: What should replace a habit you want to stop, and what does a slip tell you?
criteria: A competing response attached to the same cue — the habit is replaced, not deleted
A slip is evidence about the design, not about the person

lessons.title: Decay, and deciding what deserves maintenance

topics.title: Knowledge decay and choosing what deserves maintenance

lessons.model: Everything decays; maintenance is a budget. The question is not "how do I keep all of it" but "which of this will I need to produce, and when". Material you will look up does not need to be held.
lessons.when_to_use: Whenever a review queue grows faster than it can be cleared.
lessons.when_not_to_use: As a reason to abandon foundations. Prerequisites of everything you keep are maintained first.
lessons.worked_example: Three tiers written down: produce from memory (maintain on a schedule), recognise and locate (light review), look up when needed (no review, keep the reference note). Half the deck is retired into the third tier.
lessons.exercise: Sort twenty items into those three tiers and write the rule you used, so the next sort does not require starting again.
lessons.judging_results: The queue should shrink in proportion to what you retired, and nothing in tier one should lapse. A queue that stays the same size has not been triaged.
lessons.traps: Treating all knowledge as equally worth keeping; retiring something that everything else depends on.

retrieval_check.question: What three tiers of knowledge are useful, and what does each require?
criteria: Produce from memory — scheduled maintenance
Recognise and locate — light review
Look up when needed — no review, keep the reference

lessons.title: Two undefined methods, and question-led focus

topics.title: Survive-and-thrive filtering as a source-named technique requiring definition
Inquiry-based learning and question-led focus
Order control and sequencing as source-named techniques requiring definition

lessons.model: Two techniques in this curriculum arrive as names without definitions. Their underlying problems are recognisable — deciding what a source is worth before spending time on it, and choosing the order in which parts are learned — and both can be worked on with methods that are described openly. Inquiry-based learning inverts the usual sequence: hold a question and read against it.
lessons.when_to_use: Choosing what to study from a source, and deciding sequence.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Reading against a question you have not yet earned. Without enough background, the question is a guess and the reading misses the structure.
lessons.worked_example: Before a long source: write one question worth an hour, and one sentence on why this source might answer it. Order: prerequisites first, then the part that yields the most reusable idea, then the rest only if the question persists.
lessons.exercise: Take a source you intend to read. Write the question, the order you will read it in, and what would make you stop.
lessons.judging_results: The result is time not spent on low-value material, plus an answer you can state. If you finished the source and cannot state the answer, the question was not doing any work.
lessons.traps: Inventing a procedure for a named method and presenting it as the method; choosing an order by the source's own chapter numbering without checking prerequisites.

retrieval_check.question: What do you do when a named technique has no supplied definition?
criteria: Do not fabricate its steps or provenance
Identify the learning problem it addresses
Use an independently supported method for that problem, and say so

lessons.title: Chunking, maps, and integrating across domains

topics.title: Conceptual chunking and the limits of overcompression
Mind mapping for relationships, not decoration
Rapid self-testing from maps or diagrams
Integrating concepts across domains

lessons.model: A chunk is a group of items retrievable as one unit, which is why compression helps — until the chunk is so compressed that its parts can no longer be recovered. A map is a claim about relationships, so its arrows should be labelled and testable; a map you cannot be tested from is decoration.
lessons.when_to_use: Material with many parts and relationships; revision that keeps fragmenting.
lessons.when_not_to_use: As the first pass over unfamiliar material. Mapping before understanding produces a tidy drawing of a wrong model.
lessons.worked_example: A map of five concepts with labelled edges ("causes", "requires", "contradicts"). Then the map is covered and redrawn from memory; the differences are the revision content, not the original drawing.
lessons.exercise: Draw a labelled map of six concepts from two different subjects, then redraw it from memory and list what you lost.
lessons.judging_results: Redraw accuracy and the number of relationships you can state verbally. Neatness is not a measure.
lessons.traps: Overcompressing until the parts are gone; drawing maps you never test yourself from; connecting subjects with edges you cannot justify.

retrieval_check.question: How do you test yourself from a map, and what makes an edge meaningful?
criteria: Cover it and redraw from memory; compare and treat the differences as the content
An edge names a relationship you can justify (causes, requires, contrasts with)

lessons.title: Prioritising when you do not have the information

topics.title: Prioritisation under deadlines and incomplete information

lessons.model: With incomplete information, order by consequence and reversibility rather than by certainty. Do the thing that is expensive to get wrong and hard to undo first; defer what you can learn more about cheaply.
lessons.when_to_use: Deadlines with several unfinished pieces and no clear picture.
lessons.when_not_to_use: When the highest-consequence item is also the one you understand least — then the first action is a small probe, not the whole task.
lessons.worked_example: Three assignments, two weeks: the one that gates the others is scheduled first even though it is not the most enjoyable, and the one whose brief may still change is deferred by a week with a question sent today.
lessons.exercise: List what is outstanding. Mark each as reversible or not, and what you would learn by waiting. Reorder.
lessons.judging_results: You should be able to say, for each deferral, what you are waiting to learn. A deferral with no such sentence is avoidance wearing a schedule.
lessons.traps: Prioritising by due date when a later deadline gates an earlier one; treating uncertainty as a reason to postpone all decisions.

retrieval_check.question: What two properties decide order when information is incomplete?
criteria: Consequence (how expensive to get wrong)
Reversibility (how hard to undo)
What you would learn by waiting

lessons.title: Attention, cognitive load, and rest that is actually rest

topics.title: Attention management and reducing context switching
Managing cognitive load and overload
Focus, flow and suitable rest intervals
Energy-aware planning and protecting recovery

lessons.model: Every context switch costs re-entry time that is not visible in the schedule. Cognitive load has a ceiling set by the material and the learner, and rest restores attention only when it is not also loading it — scrolling does not count as recovery.
lessons.when_to_use: Designing a study week, and after noticing the same paragraph read three times.
lessons.when_not_to_use: As an argument against difficulty. Load from the material's complexity is the work; load from a bad interface, a noisy room or fifteen tabs is the waste.
lessons.worked_example: Two 40-minute blocks with one 10-minute walk, phone in another room, one tab open. Work that needs decisions (problem sets) scheduled in the morning; retrieval in the afternoon when it is harder but less decision-heavy.
lessons.exercise: For one day, record each switch (what interrupted, how long to re-enter). Name the two most expensive and remove one.
lessons.judging_results: Fewer switches and shorter re-entry times. A day that felt busy with no increase in output is the signal, not the noise.
lessons.traps: Treating rest as another task to optimise; confusing flow with a plan that has no stopping condition.

retrieval_check.question: What is the difference between useful load and wasted load, and what makes rest restorative?
criteria: Useful load comes from the material's intrinsic complexity
Wasted load comes from environment, interface and task switching
Rest is restorative when it does not itself demand attention

lessons.title: Systems that cost more than they save

topics.title: Avoiding productivity systems that cost more time than they save

lessons.model: A productivity system has a cost: maintenance, decisions, upkeep. It pays only if the time it returns exceeds the time it takes, measured in work produced rather than in system completeness.
lessons.when_to_use: When maintaining the system has become a category of work.
lessons.when_not_to_use: As a reason to abandon structure entirely. The failure is a system too expensive for its job, not the idea of having one.
lessons.worked_example: Three tools became one page and one calendar. Two recurring reviews became one weekly audit. The saved minutes go into a problem set — otherwise the simplification is just a tidier way to do the same amount of nothing.
lessons.exercise: List every system you maintain in a week and the minutes each takes. Cut the one with the worst ratio and record what the time went to.
lessons.judging_results: Look for the saved time appearing in output. If nothing replaced it, the simplification was cosmetic.
lessons.traps: Replacing a heavy system with a new lighter system that needs setting up for a fortnight; measuring the system's elegance instead of its yield.

retrieval_check.question: How do you judge whether a productivity system is worth its cost?
criteria: Compare time returned against time spent maintaining it
The measure is work produced, not system completeness

lessons.title: Card selection and pruning

topics.title: Flashcard selection, pruning and review management

lessons.model: A deck is a maintenance liability. Each card is a promise to review it forever, so it must earn its place: atomic, hard to guess, and worth producing from memory.
lessons.when_to_use: Building or pruning any deck.
lessons.when_not_to_use: For material whose value is in the shape of the argument. Cards atomise, and some knowledge does not survive atomisation.
lessons.worked_example: A paragraph about a mechanism becomes three cards: the mechanism's trigger, its consequence, and the exception. Anything that only needed recognising is deleted.
lessons.exercise: Prune one deck by a third. For each deletion, write the reason in one word (duplicate, trivial, unclear, not needed).
lessons.judging_results: Review time drops and delayed recall holds. A deck that shrank and whose recall improved was over-full, not under-full.
lessons.traps: Keeping a card because deleting it feels like losing knowledge; splitting one idea into six cards that are individually unanswerable.

retrieval_check.question: What does each card commit you to, and what happens to a deck that ignores it?
criteria: Ongoing maintenance — every card is a promise to review it
An unpruned deck becomes unmaintainable, and then abandoned

lessons.title: Spatial memory, rote, and where memorisation is unsafe

topics.title: The method of loci and when spatial mnemonics may be appropriate
Memorising detailed material without replacing understanding
Correct and incorrect uses of rote memorisation
Ethical and safe limits when memorising clinical, technical or high-stakes procedures

lessons.model: The method of loci binds items to a route you already know, which works well for ordered lists and poorly for anything that needs to be reasoned about. Rote is correct for exact strings and unsafe wherever the cost of a misremembered step is harm.
lessons.when_to_use: Ordered lists, exact terminology, and procedural steps that must be reproduced verbatim.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Replacing understanding. A memorised explanation you cannot defend deteriorates into a confident sentence detached from its evidence.
lessons.worked_example: A twelve-step protocol is placed along a familiar route, then each step is rehearsed with its reason attached. The route fixes the order; the reasons prevent the order from being applied to the wrong case.
lessons.exercise: Memorise an ordered list of eight items with a route, then reproduce it a day later with the reason for two of them.
lessons.judging_results: Order accuracy a day later, plus the ability to explain why the order is what it is. Order without reason is a hazard in applied material.
lessons.traps: Using memory palaces for material that needs explanation; memorising a clinical or technical step without its indications, contraindications and the fact that you are not yet qualified to apply it.

retrieval_check.question: When does rote memorisation become unsafe?
criteria: When a misremembered step causes harm or removal of judgement
When it replaces understanding of why the step exists
Names that clinical/technical procedures need indications and limits, not just steps

lessons.title: Whole, part, whole

topics.title: Whole-Part-Whole reteaching

lessons.model: See the whole once for orientation, take one part apart until it is understood, then rebuild the whole from what you have. The final step is the one usually skipped, and it is the one that produces understanding of how the parts depend on each other.
lessons.when_to_use: Complex systems, arguments and procedures with many interacting parts.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Very small material, where the whole is the part and the cycle is overhead.
lessons.worked_example: A compiler: run one program end to end (whole), then take the parser alone (part), then explain the program's journey again with the parser's input and output named (whole). The second whole is where the dependencies appear.
lessons.exercise: Choose a system you are studying. Do the three passes in one sitting and write what you could not explain in the first whole that you can explain now.
lessons.judging_results: The second whole should be materially more connected than the first. If you can only report the part in detail, the reassembly did not happen.
lessons.traps: Stopping after the part because it felt productive; treating the first whole as understanding rather than orientation.

retrieval_check.question: What does the third pass add that the first two do not?
criteria: Rebuilt whole from memory, showing dependencies between parts
The first whole is orientation only, not comprehension

lessons.title: Self-explanation, teaching, and multilevel recall

topics.title: Self-explanation and teaching a concept clearly
Multilevel conceptual recall

lessons.model: Explaining forces every gap into the open, because a sentence you cannot finish is a gap you cannot see while rereading. Multilevel recall is the same idea applied to depth: state it in one line, then a paragraph, then with the mechanism and its exceptions.
lessons.when_to_use: After a first pass, and whenever understanding feels fluent but thin.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Before any encoding. Explaining from nothing produces a confident summary of your own assumptions.
lessons.worked_example: One minute: what is entropy, in one sentence. Five minutes: the paragraph, with the mechanism. Then, with the page closed, the statement a colleague would challenge — and the answer.
lessons.exercise: Explain one concept at three depths, recorded spoken, without notes. Then transcribe and mark where you stalled.
lessons.judging_results: Where you stalled is the content of the next session. Smooth delivery at one depth and collapse at another is the normal, useful result.
lessons.traps: Explaining to yourself in the language of the source; mistaking fluency for depth; teaching a simplified version you would not defend.

retrieval_check.question: Why does explanation reveal gaps that rereading does not?
criteria: Producing language requires reconstruction; recognising text does not
A sentence you cannot finish localises the gap

lessons.title: Reconstructing, transferring, and correcting the model

topics.title: Reconstructing a complex system or argument from memory
Integration across topics and transfer to unfamiliar problems
Identifying reasoning errors and correcting the underlying model

lessons.model: Rebuilding a system or argument from memory tests structure rather than details. Transfer tests whether the structure was abstracted or only bound to the example, and a recurring error usually belongs to the model rather than to the instance.
lessons.when_to_use: Late in a topic, and whenever the same mistake appears in new material.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Early, when there is no structure yet to rebuild. Reconstruction of a half-learned system produces a plausible fiction.
lessons.worked_example: Blank page: draw the argument's premises, inference and conclusion, then the objection that would break it. Then apply the same structure to a case from another subject and see whether the inference survives.
lessons.exercise: Reconstruct one argument from memory, then find a case from a different domain where the same reasoning applies or fails.
lessons.judging_results: Structure reproduced, objection identified, and a transfer case correctly classified. Failing the transfer while passing the recall means the structure was example-bound.
lessons.traps: Correcting the instance instead of the model; treating transfer failure as a memory problem when it is an abstraction problem.

retrieval_check.question: What does a transfer failure tell you that a recall success does not?
criteria: That the structure was bound to the original example, not abstracted
The correction belongs to the model, not to the instance

lessons.title: Cramming, and multi-pass under restricted time

topics.title: The trade-offs and limits of cramming
Multi-pass methods for complex material or restricted time

lessons.model: Cramming produces availability now and decay later; it is a rational choice for a test tomorrow and a poor one for knowledge you need in six weeks. Under restricted time, several short passes with retrieval between them beat one long read, because each pass starts from what survived the last.
lessons.when_to_use: When time is genuinely short, and when choosing how to spend the last two days.
lessons.when_not_to_use: As the default. A cramming habit that works for assessments is exactly how material becomes unavailable when it is needed later.
lessons.worked_example: Two days: pass one, whole structure (60 min); pass two, retrieval on the structure (30 min); pass three, only what failed (30 min); pass four, one timed question. Reading continuously for two days replaces all four passes with one.
lessons.exercise: Plan a two-day recovery for one subject as passes with retrieval between them, and name what you are deliberately not covering.
lessons.judging_results: Performance on a delayed question, not on tomorrow's. If nothing is retained a week later, the cramming bought the assessment and nothing else — which is a decision to make knowingly.
lessons.traps: Confusing familiarity from a long read with retention; planning passes so tight that no retrieval fits between them.

retrieval_check.question: What does cramming buy, what does it cost, and what replaces it under time pressure?
criteria: Buys short-term availability, costs delayed retention
Multiple passes with retrieval between them
Knowingly choosing it rather than defaulting to it

lessons.title: The next best action, and executing under exam conditions

topics.title: Choosing the next best action when time is scarce
Exam execution: question interpretation, pacing and checking
Reducing avoidable or 'silly' errors
Deciding what not to learn and what can safely be deferred

lessons.model: With ten minutes left, the best action is the one with the highest expected gain per minute, not the one you were doing. In an exam, most avoidable loss comes from misreading the question, allocating time badly and not checking the units — all three are trainable.
lessons.when_to_use: Any assessment, and any week with more material than time.
lessons.when_not_to_use: Deciding what not to learn in a subject that is foundational to everything after it. Deferral is for the periphery.
lessons.worked_example: Exam plan written in the first two minutes: question count, marks, minutes per mark, and the order chosen so the highest-value section is done while attention is best. A final five minutes is reserved for checking units, signs and whether every question was answered.
lessons.exercise: Do one past paper under time with a written plan, then classify every lost mark as knowledge, misreading, timing or checking.
lessons.judging_results: The classification tells you what to fix. Losing marks to misreading while knowing the content is a different problem from not knowing it, and more cheaply solved.
lessons.traps: Practising content you already know because it feels good; spending the checking time re-doing the question instead of checking it.

retrieval_check.question: What are the four categories of lost marks, and why separate them?
criteria: Knowledge, misreading, timing, checking
They have different fixes; only one of them is a content problem

lessons.title: Efficiency measured later

topics.title: Evaluating efficiency by delayed outcomes, not time alone

lessons.model: Efficiency is output per unit of effort measured at a delay, because the immediate measures — pages read, hours logged, cards reviewed — all reward activity. A method that feels slow and produces recall in two weeks is more efficient than one that feels fast and produces nothing.
lessons.when_to_use: Comparing two methods, and reviewing a month.
lessons.when_not_to_use: As a reason to abandon a method after one week. Delayed outcomes need the delay to have passed.
lessons.worked_example: Two topics, two methods, one month. Both are tested cold after three weeks by the same kind of question. The method that felt worse and scored the same is the one to keep — it cost less.
lessons.exercise: Pick two comparable topics and two methods. Write now what you will test, and when, before you start.
lessons.judging_results: A delayed, unsupported test. Anything measured during the learning week is measuring the method's comfort, not its yield.
lessons.traps: Measuring hours; concluding from n=1 without saying so; changing two things at once and crediting the one you preferred.

retrieval_check.question: Why must efficiency be measured at a delay, and what must you record about the sample?
criteria: Immediate measures reward activity, not retention
The sample size and the fact it is uncontrolled, so no strong conclusion is drawn

named_methods.name: AIM
named_methods.problem: An unstated sequence for approaching or organising study of a topic.
named_methods.open_alternative: Write the sequence you actually use, name its steps, and test it against outcomes.
named_methods.note: No definition, steps, evidence or ownership supplied. Not reconstructed here.

named_methods.name: Bear Hunter System
named_methods.problem: An unstated framing for sustained effort or persistence across a long goal.
named_methods.open_alternative: Implementation intentions plus a weekly audit of what actually happened.
named_methods.note: No definition supplied. The name is vivid and the content is not, which is exactly when fabrication happens.

named_methods.name: VPReFRE criteria
named_methods.problem: Appears to be a checklist for judging a source or a piece of material.
named_methods.open_alternative: An explicit source-evaluation checklist you write and can justify: who, when, evidence, conflicts, relevance.
named_methods.note: The acronym is supplied without its expansion. Expanding it would be invention.

named_methods.name: GRINDE maps
named_methods.problem: Appears to be a mapping or structuring method for knowledge.
named_methods.open_alternative: A labelled concept map, tested by redrawing it from memory (lesson: chunking, maps and integration).
named_methods.note: No definition or example supplied. The generic mapping lesson is offered instead of a guess at the acronym.

named_methods.name: PEER-Peer
named_methods.problem: Appears to describe a peer-based or reciprocal teaching arrangement.
named_methods.open_alternative: Explain a concept to a peer and have them ask one question you cannot answer.
named_methods.note: No definition supplied. Reciprocal teaching has independent support; the named variant is not described.

named_methods.name: OFF-rest timing
named_methods.problem: Appears to concern when to stop and rest.
named_methods.open_alternative: A fixed interval that ends the block by design, with rest that does not demand attention.
named_methods.note: No timings supplied. Any number written here would be invented.

named_methods.name: survive-and-thrive filter
named_methods.problem: Deciding what a source must give you now versus what can wait.
named_methods.open_alternative: The three-tier decay triage: produce, recognise, look up.
named_methods.note: Listed in the curriculum alongside this note; no procedure was supplied.

named_methods.name: order control
named_methods.problem: Choosing the sequence in which parts of a subject are learned.
named_methods.open_alternative: Prerequisite-first ordering, with the highest-reuse idea next.
named_methods.note: The phrase is supplied; the rule is not.

named_methods.name: Huddle framework
named_methods.problem: Appears to describe a short, repeated group or self-review meeting.
named_methods.open_alternative: A five-minute weekly audit with three written lines: method used, evidence produced, one change.
named_methods.note: No definition supplied. The audit is the independently supported substitute.

dimensions.name: Mindset
practices: Respond constructively to mistakes and setbacks.
Separate task performance from personal worth or identity.
Experiment under uncertainty.
Tolerate temporary incompetence while acquiring a skill.
Recognise perfectionism, avoidance and unhelpful self-talk.
Build confidence from demonstrated competence rather than unsupported affirmation.
Analyse mistakes without turning reflection into self-criticism.
Choose a next action after a setback.
dimensions.drill: After one failed attempt this week, write two lines: what the attempt produced as evidence, and the single next action. No verdict on yourself.
dimensions.caution: These exercises are not a diagnostic tool. Do not infer a psychological condition from them, and do not treat a high reported score as proof of resilience under real pressure.

dimensions.name: Self-regulation
dimensions.goal: Monitor and change method on evidence, not on mood.
practices: Notice comprehension while learning.
Distinguish recognition, confidence, recall and application.
Monitor study methods and their results.
Use low-cost experiments to compare techniques.
Track delayed performance, error patterns and transfer.
Change strategy when the evidence warrants it.
Conduct weekly learning audits and monthly reviews.
Build self-coaching skills rather than dependence on the assistant.
dimensions.drill: Once a week, name the method you used, the evidence it produced, and one thing you will change. Record it even when nothing changes.
dimensions.caution: A weekly audit that becomes a performance review of yourself has stopped doing its job; it should judge the method, never the person.

dimensions.name: Deep processing
dimensions.goal: Build explanations that survive being questioned.
practices: Elaborate ideas in your own words.
Identify causal mechanisms and assumptions.
Compare and contrast related concepts.
Build mental models and conceptual hierarchies.
Connect concrete examples to abstract principles.
Explain when an analogy helps and where it breaks.
Find relationships across subjects.
Generate counterexamples, boundary cases and implications.
Move between verbal, visual, mathematical and procedural representations.
dimensions.drill: Take one idea you think you understand. Write its mechanism, one counterexample, and where an analogy for it stops working.
dimensions.caution: Fluency while reading is not understanding. If you cannot produce the mechanism with the page closed, the elaboration has not happened yet.

dimensions.name: Retrieval
dimensions.goal: Produce knowledge without support, and keep what survives.
practices: Practise free recall, cued recall, short answers and recognition appropriately.
Explain concepts from memory without notes.
Reconstruct diagrams, procedures, arguments and problem solutions.
Schedule retrieval across time rather than cramming into one session.
Use interleaving when it improves discrimination or transfer.
Correct errors after retrieval and later retest them.
Practise under realistic time or performance constraints when relevant.
Use flashcards selectively, alongside blank-page recall, explanation and teaching.
dimensions.drill: Blank page, five minutes, one topic: write everything, then check against the source and mark what you produced from memory.
dimensions.caution: The lowest reported score is the easiest one to over-train. Retrieval practice that never gets checked becomes rehearsal of your own errors.

dimensions.name: Self-management
dimensions.goal: A described baseline: when you start, what interrupts you, how you resume.
practices: Assess planning and prioritisation.
Assess starting and finishing tasks.
Assess procrastination and distraction.
Assess session design, context switching and decision fatigue.
Assess available time, energy, sleep, recovery and competing responsibilities.
Assess consistency, workload realism, and the ability to resume after interruption.
Create a behavioural baseline without inventing a percentage.
dimensions.drill: Complete the self-management baseline: nine self-report items plus one timed observation task. It produces a description and counts, never a score.
dimensions.caution: No percentage is computed here, by design. A number would imply a measurement that never took place.

processes.name: Priming
processes.trains: Activating prior knowledge, previewing structure, establishing a question, checking prerequisites, spotting what matters, reducing avoidable overload.
processes.drill: Six minutes, timer visible: what do I already know, what is this for, what do I need first?
processes.fails_when: It has no time budget and becomes preparation as procrastination — reorganising notes instead of starting.

processes.name: Encoding
processes.trains: Meaning construction, explanatory elaboration, organisation, examples, relationship mapping, worked-example analysis, note-making that is written for a question you will ask later.
processes.drill: Explain the mechanism in your own words to an imagined reader, then find the sentence you cannot defend.
processes.fails_when: Fluent reading is mistaken for understanding; the page feels familiar and the mechanism was never built.

processes.name: Reference
processes.trains: Deciding what is worth capturing for later lookup, what must be learned rather than stored, and what need not be saved at all. Concise notes, source attribution, definitions, mechanisms, examples, exceptions, evidence, deduplication, linking, searchability.
processes.drill: Write one note whose purpose is to answer a specific future question, then try to answer it from the note alone.
processes.fails_when: Notes grow in volume and are never used. The test is whether a note supports later retrieval and application, not how much it contains.

processes.name: Retrieval and interleaving
processes.trains: An explicit approach per material type: factual, conceptual, comparative and application-heavy. When recognition, recall, cued prompts, free response, problem reconstruction, mixed practice and spaced review each fit.
processes.drill: Pick one topic and produce it four ways: recognition, recall, explanation, application.
processes.fails_when: Interleaving is forced where blocked practice is needed for first instruction or for a procedure that is unsafe to mix yet.

processes.name: Overlearning
processes.trains: Selective extra rehearsal for automaticity, speed, fluency, performance under pressure and high-stakes procedures — after encoding and retrieval are already adequate.
processes.drill: Name one skill worth automating and one that is not; say what the second would cost.
processes.fails_when: It is applied before the material is understood, or applied everywhere and spends the time that the next topic needed.
